rule_text: Search OFBiz installation directories (C:\*ofbiz*\*\webapp\ROOT\, C:\opt\ofbiz\*\webapp\) for .jsp web shell artifacts (CVE-2024-38856).
rationale: OFBiz is a non-default Java application not covered by standard Windows file-search catalogs; JSP artifacts in its webapp root are high-confidence post-RCE persistence indicators missed because the directory path was absent from extraction locations.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks executing credential-extraction utilities (wmic, whoami, net user, secretsdump) or WMI queries for account enumeration should be flagged as attacker_persistence (CISA AA24-109A).
rationale: Teaches INTERPRET to recognize Akira-style credential-harvesting tasks by behavioral pattern, catching obfuscated or non-obvious task names that would otherwise be dismissed as benign automation.

rule_text: JSP files in web application directories (Apache OFBiz installation paths, IIS/Tomcat web roots) and vendor software base directories for web shell persistence (CVE-2024-38856, CISA April 2026).
rationale: The JSP artifact was dropped to disk but not discovered because OFBiz and standard web-app directories weren't in the baseline file catalog; adding them enables discovery without false positives (unexpected JSP files in these locations are inherently suspicious for persistence).

rule_text: Windows scheduled tasks in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks directory and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule registry
rationale: Scheduled task locations were not in the extraction catalog, so the planner had no candidate locations to examine when investigating persistence mechanisms.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks using WMI or PowerShell for credential enumeration (Get-ADUser, Get-WmiObject Win32_*, net group) as reconnaissance (MITRE T1087), even if task names suggest legitimate diagnostics.
rationale: Adversaries craft credential-enumeration tasks that mimic diagnostic tools to evade detection; preventing misclassification requires flagging enumeration patterns regardless of task context.

rule_text: Enumerate scheduled task XML files from C:\Windows\System32\tasks\ and all subdirectories; these are common vectors for T1053.005 persistence and LOTL abuse (T1047, T1059.001).
rationale: Without this location in the extraction catalog, the pipeline cannot discover scheduled task XML containing malicious WMI or PowerShell commands, even when explicitly present on the target.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks executing WMI queries (wmic) or credential enumeration commands (Get-ADUser, etc.) are indicators of attacker persistence per CISA AA24-109A.
rationale: Credential enumeration patterns in scheduled tasks may be dismissed as legitimate administration; explicit flagging ensures they are classified as malicious persistence indicators.

rule_text: When processing supply_chain artifacts, enumerate executable files in IIS web application directories (C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ and subdirectories) for potential persistence mechanisms like web shells (MITRE T1505.003).
rationale: SAP npm supply-chain compromises deploy ASPX web shells in IIS for command execution; filesystem enumeration must include IIS paths to discover these artifacts.

rule_text: Executable script files (.php, .asp, .aspx) in IIS webroot directories are indicators of web shell deployment for persistent command execution, even without known content signatures (CISA AA24-190A).
rationale: If extracted, unexpected scripts in IIS paths might otherwise be interpreted as benign. This counter_rule ensures the interpret step flags them as persistence mechanisms consistent with APT40 early-stage TTPs.

rule_text: Include C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ and IIS application virtual directories in file persistence scans to detect web shells commonly deployed by APT40 (CISA AA24-190A).
rationale: IIS webroot paths are absent from the extraction catalog, so the planner never attempts to enumerate them. Adding these locations enables detection of PHP/ASP web shells used for persistent command execution.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks naming or executing Bitwarden CLI, accessing npm credentials, or performing token operations; supply-chain attacks abuse legitimate tooling as persistence cover (April 2026).
rationale: This task mimicked npm maintenance to appear benign; the counter-rule catches malicious intent signaled by Bitwarden + credential-harvesting operations within ostensibly legitimate toolchain tasks, blocking the semantic evasion.

rule_text: Enumerate C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ task XML files in persistence discovery; scheduled tasks are equivalent persistence vectors to registry Run keys and Windows services.
rationale: The scheduled-task location was omitted from the extract catalog, so sentinel never enumerated this disk location despite successfully classifying persistence mechanisms from registry and service sources.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks executing 'cmd.exe /c type <file> | iex' patterns are high-confidence attacker persistence, even with legitimate-sounding names or descriptions.
rationale: This is a signature Layer-4 indirect injection attack for web shell execution; benign task naming (Microsoft\RebuildSearchIndex) or description should not suppress flagging the iex-piping command.

rule_text: Correlate file path references in scheduled task descriptions with action commands to detect indirect execution patterns and multi-hop attacks.
rationale: Ensures explicit reasoning that the description (mentioning rebuild_index.aspx) links to the action (executing that file), catching attacks where malicious code lives outside the task definition.

rule_text: Flag unexpected .aspx files in web application directories or vendor application webroots as malicious web shells, even if filenames appear innocuous — strong indicator of post-exploitation persistence (CISA KEV SimpleHelp Apr-2026).
rationale: Even if the file is enumerated, interpret might dismiss .aspx as legitimate website content; counter-rule ensures suspicious web shells are classified as attacker_persistence rather than benign.

rule_text: Scan Program Files/PaperCut MF/server/webapps/ROOT/ for JSP and other web shells (CVE-2023-27351 CISA AA23-149A).
rationale: Vendor-specific PaperCut webapp directory was not in the standard location catalog, preventing the planner from examining where the JSP shell was deployed.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks that enumerate Microsoft Teams credential cache indicate attacker persistence (MuddyWater TTP, Rapid7/THN May 2026).
rationale: Sentinel detected similar credential-theft in other scheduled tasks but missed this Teams-specific pattern; this counter_rule ensures cache enumeration is flagged as malicious rather than dismissed as legitimate sync activity.

rule_text: When investigating supply-chain threats, specifically enumerate scheduled tasks for npm registry patterns (.npmrc, authentication tokens, postinstall hooks) and Node.js credential harvesting code (CanisterSprawl April 2026).
rationale: Planner may not have specifically targeted npm-related scheduled tasks during supply-chain hunting; this ensures focused extraction of CanisterSprawl artifacts in Windows task scheduler.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks containing npm registry token harvesting or .npmrc credential file access code should be classified as supply-chain persistence, not just attacker_persistence (CanisterSprawl postinstall hooks, GitGuardian April 21 2026).
rationale: Interpret found npm token harvesting in a scheduled task (finding #10) but classified it as general persistence; this rule elevates such evidence to supply-chain classification, matching the actual CanisterSprawl threat profile.

rule_text: Include C:\inetpub\wwwroot and %SystemRoot%\inetpub in file-drop scans; Mini Shai-Hulud plants .aspx web shell fallbacks there (StepSecurity, T1505.003).
rationale: inetpub directories were not in the extract catalog, preventing file-drop detection despite being the documented persistence location for this supply-chain malware.

rule_text: Enumerate files in SimpleHelp application installation directories (C:\Program Files\SimpleHelp\*, C:\Program Files (x86)\SimpleHelp\www, etc.) — post-exploitation web shells planted in vendor application webroots (CISA KEV Apr-2026).
rationale: SimpleHelp webroot was not in the extract location catalog, so planner had no reason to enumerate it; adding it directly resolves the miss without generating false positives in post-breach DFIR contexts.

rule_text: When analyzing scheduled tasks, evaluate action elements for directory-open verbs ('explore', 'open', 'edit') applied to file-system paths in addition to traditional executable actions; flag those targeting user-profile or temporary directories (CVE-2026-32202).
rationale: The planner may examine the scheduled tasks catalog but overlook non-executable action types; explicit guidance ensures folder-opening patterns—which are non-standard for persistence—are evaluated as potential NTLM-coercion staging.

rule_text: Scheduled task actions that open directories (rather than executing binaries) should be flagged as suspicious—especially those targeting user-accessible paths—as they may pre-stage .lnk files for NTLM-coercion attacks (CVE-2026-32202).
rationale: The LNK spoofing attack uses a scheduled task opening a folder containing malicious .lnk files; directory-open actions are unusual for persistence and were likely misinterpreted as benign system behavior by the interpret step.

rule_text: ASPX/ASP files in IIS directories discovered during supply-chain incident response are attacker_persistence indicators unless explicitly whitelisted; do not dismiss as benign application files.
rationale: Web shells planted in IIS by supply-chain attacks may be misclassified as legitimate application artifacts if they have normal timestamps or names; counter-rule ensures proper classification.

rule_text: Unexpected .aspx files in IIS web directories are web shell indicators; do not dismiss as benign application code even in production (Mini Shai-Hulud T1505.003).
rationale: If inetpub files were examined, ASPX would be recognized as legitimate there; the counter-rule prevents the interpreter from undercalling suspicious .aspx files as normal application components.

rule_text: PHP, ASPX, or JSP files in web-accessible directories without legitimate software vendor provenance indicate post-exploitation persistence, particularly following supply-chain compromise indicators.
rationale: Once extracted, unexpected web scripts might be misclassified as benign; this rule ensures INTERPRET flags them as persistence artifacts when supply-chain context is present, catching post-exploit web shells.

rule_text: Search Windows web root directories (C:\inetpub\wwwroot, C:\xampp\htdocs, C:\Apache*\htdocs) and web application paths for PHP, ASPX, JSP files; supply-chain compromises often persist via web shells.
rationale: The PHP web shell was missed because IIS and common web root directories were not enumerated by EXTRACT; adding them ensures candidate files in web-accessible locations are captured for analysis.

rule_text: Enumerate Windows scheduled task XML definitions from C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ (system) and C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\* (user-created tasks) as persistence sources.
rationale: Missed artifact is typed scheduled_task_xml; these standard Windows task storage locations were not in the extract catalog, preventing discovery of task-based persistence.

rule_text: Scan IIS content directories (C:\inetpub\wwwroot, C:\Program Files\*\wwwroot, web application subdirectories) for dynamic content handlers (.php, .aspx, .jsp) indicating post-compromise web shells (UAT-8099).
rationale: The PHP web shell was in an IIS default content directory that the extraction catalog did not enumerate; adding this location family enables discovery of web shell persistence artifacts hidden in legitimate application paths.

rule_text: Flag .jsp files in GitHub Actions runner or CI/CD temporary directories as attacker_persistence—they enable persistent command execution for credential theft in compromised CI pipelines (Unit42 Apr 2026).
rationale: Even after finding the JSP in a GitHub Actions directory, interpret must not dismiss it as benign developer artifact; this rule ensures correct classification.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks that trigger folder-open operations (which render contained LNK file icons) as suspicious for Shell spoofing NTLM coercion (CVE-2026-32202).
rationale: Such tasks appear benign but automatically trigger LNK icon rendering, enabling NTLM authentication coercion without user interaction; this pattern must be explicitly flagged.

rule_text: Search SimpleHelp installation webroot directories (C:\Program Files\SimpleHelp\web, C:\inetpub\...) for unexpected scripting files (.aspx, .php, .shell) with recent timestamps (CISA KEV April 2026).
rationale: SimpleHelp CVSS 9.9 arbitrary upload vulnerability targets webroot; adding paths to extraction catalog enables detection of planted web shells.

rule_text: Flag .aspx and .shell files in SimpleHelp directories as attacker_persistence; arbitrary upload functionality enables persistent web shell access.
rationale: ASPX web shells uploaded via SimpleHelp exploit would persist if not flagged; such files are rare in legitimate content.

rule_text: Include C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ and registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\ in the disk-persistence catalog to enumerate scheduled task definitions.
rationale: The missed artifact was typed scheduled_task_xml; adding these standard task storage paths to the extraction catalog enables the planner to discover malicious scheduled task definitions.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks with command arguments containing environment variable references (e.g., %GITHUB_*, %RUNNER_*), PowerShell execution, or suspicious endpoints as attacker_persistence even if the task name appears system-related (Unit42 Apr 2026).
rationale: The missed task exfiltrated GitHub Actions runner environment state; this prevents interpret from dismissing scheduled tasks with env-var staging or external-endpoint patterns as legitimate.

rule_text: Include GitHub Actions runner directories (C:\actions-runner\, %USERPROFILE%\.github-runner\) in file-system enumeration to detect web shells planted in CI/CD environments.
rationale: The missed JSP artifact was in a GitHub Actions runner directory not covered by the default Windows persistence catalog; this rule ensures the planner searches those locations.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks executing at system startup with WMI/WMIC commands for system reconnaissance (hostname, user, share enumeration); these match Akira playbook tactics (Cyble 5/2026).
rationale: Once extracted, WMI-based reconnaissance tasks need explicit classification guidance; without it, the pattern may be dismissed as legitimate system discovery rather than attacker persistence.

rule_text: Extract all XML files from C:\Windows\System32\tasks\ directory; scheduled tasks are primary T1053 persistence vectors.
rationale: Sentinel found multiple persistence artifacts (registry, services, named pipes) but not scheduled tasks, indicating task XML paths aren't in the extraction catalog; this location covers the primary scheduled task storage.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks in C:\Windows\System32\tasks\ with 'npm', 'node', 'preinstall', or .npmrc in names or command arguments should be extracted as supply-chain persistence candidates (GitGuardian Apr 2026).
rationale: The planner likely enumerated scheduled tasks generically, but the extract catalog lacked npm-specific patterns, so this artifact fell outside the candidate set examined by interpret.

rule_text: Flag scheduled tasks and registry entries mentioning npm preinstall hooks, .npmrc paths, or environment variable harvesting of GitHub/npm tokens as persistence, not legitimate package management (GitGuardian Apr 2026).
rationale: Even if extracted, the interpret step may have dismissed npm-related tasks as benign; this rule ensures token-harvesting context overrides that assumption.

rule_text: When on-host LLM services (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM ports 8000, 11434, 5000) are detected, immediately enumerate Task Scheduler and cron jobs for periodic network operations to those endpoints.
rationale: Planner found the LLM service but did not correlate it with task persistence checks; this rule creates that dependency, avoiding independent misses when only the LLM is visible.

rule_text: Examine ActiveMQ webroot directories (C:\Program Files\ActiveMQ\webapps\*) for unauthorized file drops; CVE-2026-34197 Jolokia gadget exploitation plants JSP web shells there (THN April 2026).
rationale: ActiveMQ webroot paths were absent from the extraction location catalog, so the planner never enumerated the dropped JSP; adding this vendor-specific location enables artifact discovery.

rule_text: Flag JSP files discovered in ActiveMQ webroot directories as suspicious persistence artifacts; CVE-2026-34197 Jolokia gadget plants command-execution web shells there (THN April 2026).
rationale: If the JSP was found during extraction, it would be classified as benign application code without this rule; the counter-rule flags suspicious web shells in vendor webroots even without file-hash IOCs.

rule_text: Windows services with Java classpaths or .JAR loading from non-standard paths (ProgramData, Temp, user AppData) are persistence mechanisms (Horizon3 Apr 2026).
rationale: Service registry evidence was likely enumerated but interpret dismissed modified Java classpath as benign; rule ensures Java classpath abuse is flagged as malicious.

rule_text: When enumerating Windows service persistence, specifically check services with ImagePath containing java.exe or service names matching ActiveMQ, Tomcat, JBoss, broker patterns.
rationale: Planner may not have recognized Java application services as compromise targets; this ensures ActiveMQ broker hijacking and similar Java persistence is discovered.

rule_text: Include C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ in persistence enumeration—scheduled tasks are persistent post-exploitation mechanisms in lateral movement campaigns (CVE-2026-4670, CVE-2026-5174).
rationale: Scheduled task directory missing from extraction catalog prevented discovery; adding it directly addresses (b)-type miss with low false-positive risk since malicious tasks carry conspicuous reconnaissance payloads.

rule_text: Flag Windows scheduled tasks making repeated queries to local LLM endpoints (127.0.0.1:11434, localhost:8000+) or sending host reconnaissance data to AI services as attacker-orchestrated persistence, regardless of benign-looking task names.
rationale: The host has Ollama running (Finding #7); a task that periodically queries it is an obvious persistence+intelligence channel. This rule prevents dismissal as a benign admin utility.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks containing reconnaissance commands (LDAP queries, net view, share enumeration, dsquery) should be classified as attacker_persistence, not benign system activity.
rationale: The missed artifact executed LDAP and share enumeration for post-compromise lateral movement; counter-rule prevents interpret step from dismissing reconnaissance-pattern tasks as legitimate administrative work.

rule_text: Cisco Catalyst or SDWAN services should be flagged as persistence if their binary path (ImagePath) is not in standard Cisco directories like Program Files\Cisco, especially if in ProgramData or writable paths, per CVE-2026-20122.
rationale: Sentinel successfully detected other malicious services but likely misclassified this Cisco-branded service as benign due to legitimate vendor association; this rule ensures vendor-branded services with anomalous binary locations trigger high-confidence persistence alerts.

rule_text: Extract Windows scheduled task definitions from Task Scheduler database (C:\Windows\System32\tasks\*) and AppData locations; examine all tasks regardless of creator or naming convention.
rationale: Scheduled tasks are a native Windows persistence vector; the missed artifact hides attack orchestration in legitimate-looking periodic tasks. Without catalog inclusion, the planner never examined them.

rule_text: When investigating file-based persistence, explicitly plan to enumerate script files (.aspx, .jsp, .php) in installed CI/CD tool directories (TeamCity, Jenkins, Azure DevOps) and plugin directories.
rationale: CI/CD tool webroots represent a distinct persistence class from registry/service entries; explicit planner guidance ensures these non-standard locations are checked for webshell artifacts.

rule_text: Enumerate PHP files in cPanel and common web root directories (/home/*/public_html, /var/www, C:\Websites, C:\wwwroot) for analysis of file_drop artifacts.
rationale: PHP webshells from cPanel CVE-2026-41940 RCE persist in webroot; EXTRACT must include these locations in directory enumeration or the file never enters the evidence bundle.

rule_text: Include C:\Program Files\JetBrains\TeamCity\webapps\ROOT\ and C:\TeamCity\webapps\ROOT\ in file persistence enumeration; ASPX webshells enable CI/CD compromise (CVE-2024-27199, CISA KEV Apr 2026).
rationale: TeamCity's webroot was absent from the extraction catalog; file-based webshell persistence in CI/CD webroots requires explicit location enumeration to detect path-traversal exploitation.

rule_text: PHP files in web-accessible directories with base64 encoding, obfuscated code, or system execution functions indicate attacker persistence, not legitimate application code.
rationale: If extracted, a .php file in webroot risks dismissal as benign code; counter_rule flags RCE-indicative patterns (encoding, eval, shell exec) to ensure high-confidence classification.

rule_text: Web application directories for JSP shells: C:\inetpub\wwwroot, C:\Tomcat\webapps, /var/www/html, /opt/tomcat/webapps (CVE-2026-42208).
rationale: JSP web shells planted post-exploitation were not enumerated because web application directories were absent from the disk-persistence extraction catalog.

rule_text: JSP files in application directories are attacker persistence for post-exploitation web shell command execution (CVE-2026-42208 CISA KEV May 2026).
rationale: JSP artifacts, once extracted, must be classified as attacker_persistence rather than legitimate application code to catch LiteLLM credential-theft shells.

rule_text: Enumerate ASPX files and API key management handlers in C:\Program Files\SimpleHelp and C:\Program Files (x86)\SimpleHelp directories for unauthenticated provisioning endpoints (CVE-2024-57726).
rationale: SimpleHelp's ASPX handlers are in vendor-specific directories outside the standard web app catalog; the extraction phase never searches there, so the planner has no candidate file to examine.

rule_text: ASPX files in SimpleHelp directories that provision or manage API keys, especially those callable without authentication or role validation, indicate CVE-2024-57726 exploitation and attacker_persistence.
rationale: Even if the ASPX is extracted, interpret may dismiss it as legitimate application code; the counter_rule flags that SimpleHelp's API provisioning requires authentication, so unauthenticated access patterns are suspicious.

rule_text: SimpleHelp installation and webroot directories (C:\Program Files\SimpleHelp, C:\ProgramData\SimpleHelp, C:\inetpub\wwwroot) for web shell staging discovery.
rationale: SimpleHelp isn't in default persistence location catalogs; CVE-2024-57728 exploits ZIP extraction to application webroots, so these paths must be enumerated to find staged PHP files.

rule_text: Enumerate PHP and recently-modified ZIP files in SimpleHelp directories; web shell staging via path traversal upload (CVE-2024-57728).
rationale: Planner must know to enumerate PHP files and recent archives (not just executables/services) in SimpleHelp locations to surface staged web shell artifacts.

rule_text: PHP files in SimpleHelp web directories are attacker persistence, not application code—flag regardless of filename or path patterns (CVE-2024-57728).
rationale: If evidence surfaces, interpreter will otherwise dismiss PHP in app directories as benign; CVE-2024-57728 exploitation specifically involves uploading PHP to web-accessible paths, making these inherently suspicious.

rule_text: Enumerate scheduled tasks from C:\Windows\System32\Tasks directory and system task registry (HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache).
rationale: CrossLock ransomware persists via scheduled tasks using ETW evasion (Cyble 2026). Scheduled task locations were absent from the extraction catalog, preventing this persistence vector from being discovered.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks accessing npm credential locations (.npmrc, cache, AppData token stores) or exfiltrating credentials indicate supply-chain persistence, regardless of task name obfuscation (Shai-Hulud 2.0, Wiz May 2026).
rationale: If the scheduled task was extracted but dismissed as benign due to empty/minimal manifest data, this counter-rule ensures npm-credential-access patterns in tasks are flagged as malicious persistence rather than dismissed as legitimate tooling.

rule_text: When investigating npm/Node.js supply-chain compromises (e.g., Shai-Hulud 2.0), prioritize enumeration of Windows scheduled tasks in addition to services, as attackers use periodic task scheduling for credential exfiltration.
rationale: Sentinel found 8 service detections but zero scheduled task findings despite the artifact being scheduled_task_xml, indicating the planner did not call scheduled task enumeration; this ensures task enumeration is prioritized for npm supply-chain investigations.

rule_text: Extract scheduled task XML files from C:\Windows\Tasks\ and C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ directories for lolbin_abuse investigation.
rationale: Scheduled task XML locations weren't in extraction catalog, preventing discovery of task-based persistence used in multi-stage privilege escalation (Arctic Wolf CherryLoader April 2026).

rule_text: When investigating lolbin_abuse or process ghosting, explicitly query Windows Task Scheduler and examine task XML for suspicious execution paths or parent process patterns.
rationale: Planner wasn't querying Windows Task Scheduler during lolbin_abuse investigation, missing CherryLoader's scheduled task bootstrap (Arctic Wolf April 2026).

rule_text: Scheduled tasks containing encryption-related binaries, obfuscated parameters, or ETW-disabling function calls represent attacker persistence even if task names appear legitimate.
rationale: Even if scheduled tasks are extracted, they may be dismissed as benign system configuration. This counter-rule escalates suspicious scheduled tasks to persistence findings rather than dismissing them.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks with encrypted binary payloads or obfuscated executable configurations should be classified as attacker_persistence; encrypted configs in task XMLs indicate malware rather than legitimate automation (VECT 2.0, THN April 2026).
rationale: Encrypted payload configs in scheduled task definitions are exclusive to malware; this rule prevents interpret-step misclassification if the task is located, ensuring encrypted-payload tasks are not dismissed as benign administrative configuration.

rule_text: Windows scheduled task XML files in C:\Windows\System32\tasks\ and subdirectories may contain encrypted binary configurations for malware persistence; enumerate task definitions for suspicious execution patterns.
rationale: Sentinel discovered six service-based persistence indicators but lacked scheduled task XML locations in its extraction catalog; VECT 2.0's task-based execution mechanism was never a candidate location for analysis.

rule_text: When investigating LOLBIN abuse for persistence, examine Windows Task Scheduler for MSBuild.exe invocations with external .csproj files or DLL sideloading patterns (Fortinet Feb-May 2026).
rationale: The planner found multiple persistence indicators (registry, services) but did not examine Task Scheduler; this rule ensures scheduled tasks are checked in LOLBIN persistence hunts, catching MSBuild-based attack chains.

rule_text: IIS web root directories (C:\inetpub\wwwroot\, C:\Program Files\*\wwwroot\, C:\websites\, C:\inetpub\temp\) where ASP.NET web shells and phishing pages are staged as persistence mechanisms.
rationale: Web shells are placed in web-accessible directories outside default system paths; cataloging these locations lets the planner discover ASP.NET files that would otherwise go unsearched.

rule_text: For apt_specific_ttp file_drop artifacts, enumerate .aspx files in web directories and analyze form handlers for credential collection patterns and POST requests to non-Microsoft endpoints (MuddyWater May 2026).
rationale: The empty manifest left the planner without direction to search for web shells; this hint ensures it proactively searches web directories for credential-harvesting ASP.NET files when file_drop persistence is suspected.

rule_text: When IDE credential caches (.vscode, .claude, .aws, .azure, .env) are discovered, explicitly enumerate web-accessible root directories and IIS installations for anomalous .aspx, .asmx, or executable files planted for credential harvesting.
rationale: The Shai-Hulud attack pattern plants web shells alongside credential harvesting; correlating these indicators ensures the planner searches for ASPX files when development-environment credential stores are detected.

rule_text: Scan C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ XML files and Registry scheduled-task caches for BitLocker recovery environment invocations (GreenPlasma ZD).
rationale: Scheduled task XML persistence locations may not be in the extraction catalog; empty manifest indicates planner did not enumerate task files, so counter_rule and planner_hint cannot fire.

rule_text: BitLocker recovery environment or recovery partition operations in scheduled tasks indicate SYSTEM privilege escalation; do not classify as legitimate Windows maintenance.
rationale: If task was extracted, prevents interpret from dismissing it as benign system operation; BitLocker recovery invocation is not a maintenance operation and indicates privilege escalation intent.

rule_text: Enumerate Windows scheduled tasks and extract C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\*.xml for supply-chain attack patterns, especially targeting npm/pnpm/pip dependencies (Wiz May 2026).
rationale: Scheduled tasks provide reliable persistence for periodic supply-chain attacks; supply-chain adversaries use them to maintain pnpm-store poisoning and achieve self-propagating worm behavior.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks with payloads targeting ~/.pnpm-store/, ~/.npm-cache/, or pip caches for injection/poisoning should be flagged as attacker_persistence (Wiz May 2026).
rationale: Cache injection patterns in scheduled task definitions are definitive indicators of supply-chain compromise, regardless of task naming; this pattern is specific enough to avoid flagging legitimate package manager maintenance tasks.

rule_text: Windows Scheduled Tasks XML files in C:\Windows\System32\tasks\ and related task registry locations.
rationale: Scheduled tasks are a primary persistence mechanism; ensuring extraction from standard directories allows evaluation of task commands for threat indicators.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks enumerating SCADA software credential stores (Wonderware, Siemens TIA, GE Digital) or containing credential-harvesting/DNS-exfil commands are attacker_persistence (CISA AA26-097A).
rationale: Identifies Iranian APT SCADA-targeting persistence patterns that would otherwise be dismissed as routine engineering software activity.

rule_text: Windows scheduled task XML files in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ may contain persistence malware; examine all .xml files for certutil, PowerShell invocations, and suspicious external commands.
rationale: Scheduled tasks are a standard persistence vector but likely absent from the extract catalog; adding this path ensures the planner enumerates the location where this certutil task was stored.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks executing certutil to download and base64-decode payloads for PowerShell invocation is LOLBIN abuse for attacker persistence (Hive Security May 2026), not benign system administration.
rationale: Even if the task XML was extracted, this specific certutil+base64+PowerShell pattern must be flagged as high-confidence attacker_persistence, not dismissed as routine utility usage.

rule_text: Scheduled tasks making API calls to Session messenger service for credential exfiltration are malicious, even if disguised by legitimate-looking names or intervals (Wiz May 2026).
rationale: The Session messenger exfiltration pattern might be overlooked as a benign external API call; this counter-rule ensures credential-exfil + Session API patterns are flagged as attacker persistence.
